newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND-Euro airlines face new lost cost era in '9.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Euro airlines face new lost cost era in '9.

text.p: The battle for control of Europe's skies will increase in 1997 when the European Union completes deregulation of its aviation market to allow any airline to fly anywhere for any price.

The final barrier will be lifted in April when EU countries must open up their domestic air markets to free competition. Industry experts say that Europe will be spared the massacre that followed liberalisation in the U.S. industry 18 years ago, when dozens of new low cost airlines descended on the majors, only to disappear in a corporate bloodbath.

"The airports that command high yield business traffic are now essentially full, giving the incumbent airlines an enviable degree of protection," said Guy Kekwick, European airlines analyst at Lehman Brothers.
"But this does not mean that a happy status quo will exist between state carriers and start-up carriers and in areas where the two overlap we expect intense competition for market share."

At the very least industry analysts say low-cost carriers in Europe can only add to the pressure on the majors next year to cut their own costs and seek ways to spin out their networks by forging more alliances, by franchising and possibly by merger.

After a year of strong passenger growth and rising fuel costs Europe's major airlines face a mixed outlook for 1997 with rising demand likely to nourish the strong but stifle the inefficient, say analysts.
OPERATING PROFITS UNDER PRESSURE

Kekwick said the trend was already evident this year, where even operating profits at leading airlines such as British Airways, KLM and Lufthansa all showed declines despite a generally buoyant market.
This was due partly to a sharp rise in the price of fuel and because they are also struggling to cope with the rising costs of having to handle extra traffic, he said.

Professor Rigas Doganis, head of the Department of Air Transport at Cranfield University, England, and former head of Olympic Airways, says that even if the first wave of low-cost carriers perishes their legacy is already assured. He says the majors, led by British Airways, are now moving

towards using low cost operators to set new standards of efficiency in their own companies. In particular they will draw on the key concept pioneered by Southwest Airlines in the United States, and now adopted by start-up airlines in Europe such as British-based carrier EasyJet, of buying in ancillary services such as baggage handling and check-in and aircraft maintenance.
OUTSOURCING

"I think 1997 is going to be the year of outsourcing. It is the year when everyone will try and see how much they can cut costs further, either by outsourcing or by relocation, by moving their employees to other, low wage economies," he told Reuters.

Meanwhile the airlines already pioneering the low-cost trail in Europe say they are confident they can succeed, despite the widespread view that established operators are protected by congestion at their most important hubs.
They say cheaper secondary airports allow them to get a foothold with bargain-basement fares which attract as much new business as they take from existing services.
And use of regional airports means they can avoid an early all-out war which they would face if they operated out of a major airline's home hub airport.
CHEAP FARES ATTRACT MORE TRAVELLERS

"If you offer cheap fares everyone finds an excuse to travel," said EasyJet founder Stelios Haji-Ioannou. "There is going to be a proliferation of low cost carriers and there are going to be casualties, but the casualties are going to be those who try to take the majors head on and don't look for niches," he said.

Since it was launched just over a year ago EasyJet has put its four brash orange Boeing 737s to work on six routes out of Luton airport north of London, to Edinburgh, Glasgow, Aberdeen and Amsterdam, Nice and Barcelona.

Haji-Ioannou offers to fly customers for less than the price of a pair of jeans and says his flights average 59 percent loadings, with Barcelona rising to 99 percent last summer and Edinburgh consistently running above 70 percent.
Having proved the concept works, he said he is now negotiating to buy another five used 737-300s for expansion and also plans to extend flights from Luton to link up his continental destinations.

"That will be an interesting development for us next year," he said. "We fly London to Amsterdam. Now there is nothing stopping me putting on a flight from Amsterdam to Nice with the same plane as a through-flight."
LOW-COST CARRIERS EXPAND SERVICES

Debonair, another new carrier based at Luton took off last June and now serves the northern English city of Newcastle and a series of connecting routes across Europe including Duesseldorf, Munich, Barcelona, Madrid, Rome and Copenhagen with all one-way fares pegged below 50 pounds ($82.50).
Debonair's chairman and U.S. industry veteran Franco Mancassola said the company is now looking at expanding domestic services in Europe, including Italy and Germany.

"We fly within Germany, within Spain, between Germany and Spain, between Italy and Spain and between Italy and Germany and we have done that so that we don't go head-to-head with any one particular major carrier," he told Reuters.
MAJORS TAKE TIPS FROM LOW-COST CARRIERS

Mancassola is particularly wary of British Airways which has led the way on rationalisation among the majors and now wants to recast itself in the mould of low-cost carriers by overhauling its cost structure.

But he said newcomers developing their cost base from scratch will be able to take market from major airlines on the continent who continue to struggle to get to grips with their historically unwieldy cost structures.

"I have the greatest respect for BA and they may be able to accomplish it. But there are others who remain dinosaurs, and I can't see a dinosaur trying to get into a lizard's skin. "Eventually it is possible that the big airlines will abandon routes that are shorter than a 1,000 miles (1,609 km)...because I don't believe that their cost structure is such that it will allow these routes to be profitable for them."
LOW-COST CARRIERS TO CLASH HEAD-ON WITH MAJORS

Sooner or later low cost carriers are going to confront the majors head-on, said Jonathan Ornstein, chief executive of British entrepreneur Richard Branson's new Brussels-based carrier Virgin Express.

Last month Virgin did just that, albeit under the wing of Sabena, by taking over the Belgian carrier's nine daily London Heathrow to Brussels services as a surrogate operator, flying in Virgin livery.

"I think fare yields will come down across Europe," Ornstein told Reuters. "It may take some time for that to happen because there is definitely a certain set of business traveller that is going to go on flying the flag carrier and pay five times more than he has to because he is not paying for the ticket. "But his corporate travel department will figure that one out eventually."
